summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Boyacá. A visitor to the department is therefore assessed against the national Colombian framework and the national pattern of violence, with incidents from other departments cited only as evidence of how that pattern expresses itself.

The national framework is comparatively developed. Since June 2015 trans Colombians have changed the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone, and 41 trans women were killed in 2023. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings must be addressed urgently.

Targeted killings occur in ordinary urban settings as well as in conflict-affected territory. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; the assault was filmed and the video went viral from 5 April, and she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested as of the 14 April 2025 report. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events denouncing transphobia were held in several cities. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". The same reporting recalls earlier fatal attacks on LGBT people in Colombia, including a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping and victims killed in their homes and in a hairdresser.

Armed groups continue to threaten trans women directly. In Caquetá, three armed men gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. Courts have also intervened in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between the national legal position and the reported experience of trans Colombians is the central turbulence in the available material. Legal gender recognition by notary act, constitutional protection of self-recognition and identity markers on national documents coexist with a homicide count that the Attorney General's Office put at 35 LGBTI people in the first five months of 2025.

Violence is not confined to territories where armed groups operate. The April 2025 killing of Sara Millerey took place in an ordinary urban setting in Antioquia, in broad daylight and filmed by bystanders, which indicates a risk profile that is not limited to remote or conflict-affected departments. Conversely, the Caquetá and Guajira flyer campaigns show that where armed groups are present the threat is announced in advance and names categories of people rather than individuals alone.

Economic marginalisation compounds the exposure. Reporting from Caquetá found discrimination restricting trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which narrows the options available to someone who has been ordered to leave a town and shapes how quickly a threat translates into displacement.

Colombia's trajectory is comparatively favourable within Latin America, and international monitors have said so; the UN Independent Expert praised the government's reforms even while warning of the disconnect with lived experience. The prosecutions before the Special Jurisdiction for Peace place Colombia among the few states where violence against LGBT people has been charged as gender persecution rather than ordinary homicide.

outOfScopeNotes:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding for Boyacá was located in the source inventory. Whether Boyacá has its own documented cases of violence against trans people, its own police protocols, or any departmental protection programme is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not establish whether the armed-group "social cleansing" flyer campaigns documented in Caquetá and Guajira operate in Boyacá. The presence or absence of armed groups in Boyacá, and any threat they may issue to trans residents, is unresolved.

National homicide figures are given for different periods by different sources: 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025, eight trans women killed between February and April 2024, and 41 trans women killed in 2023. These counts are not directly comparable and no consolidated national total for 2025 is available in the inventory.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved. The status of the identification markers introduced in November 2025 for foreign documents, and whether a visitor's own documents can be amended while in Colombia, is not sourced.

As of the 14 April 2025 report, no arrest had been made in the killing of Sara Millerey; the outcome of the investigation ordered by President Petro is unresolved.
